title: Lonely Integer
directAnswer: Every value appears exactly twice except one. XOR every element together: each duplicated pair cancels to 0 (because x ^ x = 0), leaving only the lonely value (because x ^ 0 = x). That is one pass, O(n) time and O(1) space — no hash map needed.

remember.pattern: XOR the whole array; pairs cancel, the loner survives
remember.formula:
result = 0
for x in arr:
    result ^= x
return result
rules: **x ^ x == 0** — any value XORed with itself vanishes. This is what makes every duplicate pair disappear.
**x ^ 0 == x** — XOR with zero is the identity, so start the accumulator at 0 and the loner passes through untouched.
XOR is **commutative and associative**, so order does not matter — you can fold the array left to right in one pass.
Start the accumulator at **0**, never at `arr[0]` unless you then skip index 0 — double-counting the first element flips the answer.
This beats counting in a hash map (O(n) space) and sorting (O(n log n)) — XOR is **O(n) time, O(1) space**.
whenToUse: Find the single unpaired element where all others pair up
Detect a missing or extra value via cancellation
You want O(1) space, not a frequency map
Pairs (or even counts) cancel and you need the odd one out
antiSignals: Some value appears three times, not twice → XOR alone won't isolate it (use bit-count mod 3)
Two distinct singletons exist → one XOR mixes them; split by a differing bit
You need the count of each element, not just the loner → use a hash map
Elements are not integers / not XOR-able → fall back to hashing
remember.takeaway: XOR is the cancellation operator: identical values annihilate, leaving the odd one standing. Lonely Integer is the cleanest use — fold the array with ^ and the answer falls out in O(1) space. The same trick powers Missing Number and Single Number II/III.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you know x ^ x = 0 and x ^ 0 = x well enough to collapse the array with a single XOR fold instead of reaching for a hash map, and whether you can articulate why the pairs cancel.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Defaulting to a frequency hash map (O(n) space) when the XOR insight gives O(1), or seeding the accumulator with arr[0] and then also XORing it in the loop, double-counting it.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: State the two XOR identities, explain that order doesn't matter so pairs cancel regardless of position, and deliver the one-line O(1)-space fold.

problemStatement:
Given an array of integers where **every element appears exactly twice except for one**, find and return that single element.

Your solution should run in linear time and, ideally, use only constant extra space.
constraints: Exactly one element appears once; every other appears exactly twice
A unique answer is guaranteed to exist
understanding: All but one value come in matched pairs. If we could make each pair erase itself, only the unpaired value would remain. XOR does exactly that: combining a value with its twin yields 0, and combining anything with 0 leaves it unchanged. So XORing the entire array collapses every pair to 0 and returns the lonely element.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Is it guaranteed that exactly one element is unpaired?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes. Every other value appears exactly twice, so the XOR of the whole array is precisely the lonely element.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can elements be zero?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes. Zero behaves like any other value: two zeros cancel, and a lonely zero is returned correctly because 0 is the XOR identity.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Does the order of the array matter?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: No. XOR is commutative and associative, so pairs cancel regardless of where they sit. A single left-to-right pass suffices.

clarifyingQuestions.question: What if I'm asked to use no extra space at all?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: XOR already uses O(1) space — one accumulator. That's the whole point over a hash map.

examples.explanation: The 1s, 2s, and 3s pair off and cancel to 0; only 4 has no partner, so the XOR of everything is 4.
A single element is its own answer: 0 ^ 7 = 7.

approaches.name: Hash Map — Count Frequencies
approaches.whenToMention: A reasonable first instinct worth stating, then beat it on space with XOR.
hints: Count how many times each value appears using a hash map.
Scan the map for the entry whose count is 1 — that's the lonely integer.
Correct and linear time, but it stores up to n/2 + 1 distinct keys: O(n) extra space.
approaches.complexityReasoning: One pass to count plus one pass over the map, both linear. The map can hold roughly half the elements, so O(n) space — the cost XOR avoids.
approaches.explanation:
The most direct reading: tally everything, then look for the value seen only once.

**Why it's the natural first idea.** 'One element appears once, the rest twice' maps cleanly onto counting. A hash map from value to frequency answers 'how many times did I see this?' in O(1) average, so one pass builds the tally and a second pass finds the count-1 entry.

**Where it falls short.** It works and runs in linear time, but it allocates a map that can grow to about half the array size — O(n) extra space. The problem hints at constant space, and an interviewer asking this is almost always looking for the XOR trick that needs none.

**Why mention it anyway.** Stating the counting approach shows you understand the problem and gives you a baseline to improve on. Then you say 'but we can avoid the map entirely' and pivot to XOR. That progression — correct-but-heavy to elegant — is what gets graded.
approaches.insight: Counting solves it but pays O(n) space. The leap is realising you don't need counts at all — you only need pairs to cancel, which XOR does for free.

approaches.name: XOR Fold — Pairs Cancel (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: The answer they want. Phrase it as 'XOR everything; twins cancel to 0, the loner remains'.
hints: Recall two facts: x ^ x = 0 and x ^ 0 = x. What happens if you XOR every element of the array together?
Each value that appears twice contributes x ^ x = 0, so all pairs vanish. The lonely value, with no twin, is left.
Start an accumulator at 0 and XOR each element into it. Return the accumulator — that's the answer, in one pass and no extra space.
approaches.complexityReasoning: A single pass performing one XOR per element — O(n) time. Just one integer accumulator — O(1) space.
approaches.explanation:
Collapse the array with XOR and let the duplicates erase themselves.

**The two identities that make it work.** XOR has two properties you must have at your fingertips: `x ^ x = 0` (a value cancels itself) and `x ^ 0 = x` (zero is the identity). Together they mean that combining any value with its twin produces 0, and combining the result with anything else leaves that thing unchanged.

**Why every pair disappears.** XOR is commutative and associative, so you can mentally reorder the array to place each value next to its twin: `(a ^ a) ^ (b ^ b) ^ ... ^ lonely`. Every parenthesised pair becomes 0, and you are left with `0 ^ 0 ^ ... ^ lonely = lonely`. The array order in the actual code does not matter — the same cancellation happens during a straight left-to-right fold.

**Why start at 0.** The accumulator must begin at the XOR identity, 0, so the first element passes through unchanged (`0 ^ arr[0] = arr[0]`). Seeding it with `arr[0]` and then also XORing `arr[0]` in the loop would cancel the first element with itself, corrupting the result. Start at 0 and fold the whole array.

**Why this beats the hash map.** No counts, no map, no second pass — one accumulator and one loop. O(n) time like the map, but O(1) space, which is exactly what the constant-space hint is steering you toward.
approaches.insight: XOR is a cancellation machine: feed it the array and matched values annihilate in pairs, leaving the unmatched one. The accumulator starting at 0 is not arbitrary — 0 is XOR's identity, the only safe seed.

dryRun.intro: Fold left to right starting from 0; watch pairs cancel as they meet.

java.explanation: Seed with the XOR identity so the first element passes through unchanged.
Each value meeting its twin cancels to 0; the unpaired value accumulates.
After all pairs cancel, only the lonely integer remains.

python.explanation: Start at 0, the identity element for XOR.
Fold each element in; duplicates annihilate.
The surviving value is the single unpaired element.

edgeCases.behavior: 0 ^ 7 = 7. A single element is returned directly.
0 ^ 0 ^ 5 = 5. A lonely non-zero survives even amid zero pairs.
4 ^ 5 ^ 4 = 5. Order-independent cancellation: the two 4s cancel wherever they are.

pitfalls: Seeding the accumulator with arr[0] and also XORing it in the loop — double-counts and corrupts the result.
Reaching for a hash map out of habit and missing the O(1)-space XOR.
Assuming XOR only works if duplicates are adjacent — it doesn't matter, XOR is order-independent.

commonMistakes: Using a hash map (O(n) space) when XOR solves it in O(1) space.
Initialising the XOR accumulator with arr[0] and then re-XORing arr[0] in the loop.
Believing the array must be sorted or pairs adjacent for XOR to work.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Wrong accumulator seed
commonMistakesDetailed.why: XOR's identity is 0. Seeding with arr[0] and then XORing arr[0] again in the loop cancels the first element with itself.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
int result = arr[0];
for (int x : arr) result ^= x;   // arr[0] counted twice
commonMistakesDetailed.good:
int result = 0;
for (int x : arr) result ^= x;   // every element counted once

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Defaulting to a hash map
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Counting works but costs O(n) space. The interviewer's constant-space hint points straight at XOR.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
from collections import Counter
return next(v for v, c in Counter(arr).items() if c == 1)  # O(n) space
commonMistakesDetailed.good:
result = 0
for x in arr:
    result ^= x
return result   # O(1) space

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Assuming pairs must be adjacent
commonMistakesDetailed.why: XOR is commutative and associative, so duplicates cancel no matter where they appear — sorting is unnecessary.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad: arr.sort()   # needless O(n log n); XOR doesn't need order

patternNote: XOR cancellation. When duplicates pair up and you need the odd one out, XOR the whole collection: identical values annihilate (x ^ x = 0) and the identity (x ^ 0 = x) preserves the survivor. Recurs in Missing Number, Single Number II/III, and finding a swapped pair.
